Case Study: How Does a Bike-Share Navigate Speedy Success?

Kacper Fabijański

2023-05-13

Ask - Introduction with clear statement of business task

Until now, Cyclistic’s marketing strategy relied on building general awareness and appealing to broad consumer segments. One approach that helped make these things possible was the flexibility of its pricing plans: single-ride passes, full-day passes, and annual memberships. Customers who purchase single-ride or full-day passes are referred to as casual riders. Customers who purchase annual memberships are Cyclistic members

Cyclistic’s finance analysts have concluded that annual members are much more profitable than casual riders. Although the pricing flexibility helps Cyclistic attract more customers, Lily Moreno, the director of marketing believes that maximizing the number of annual members will be key to future growth. Rather than creating a marketing campaign that targets all-new customers, Moreno believes there is a very good chance to convert casual riders into members. She notes that casual riders are already aware of the Cyclistic program and have chosen Cyclistic for their mobility needs.

Key stakeholders:

Lily Moreno: The director of marketing - responsible for the development of campaigns and initiatives to promote the bike-share program.

Marketing analytics team: responsible for collecting, analyzing, and reporting data that helps guide Cyclistic marketing strategy.

Executive team: will decide whether to approve the recommended marketing program

Business task: Identify how do annual members and casual riders use Cyclistic bikes differently.

ROCCC

R- Dataset seems to be pretty reliable - there are missing values when it comes to start and end stations - complete rate for these values is about 85% and end_lat/end_lng have about 99.8% complete rate. The rest of the values are completely accurate. O - It’s also original, because it comes directly from company tracking app so it’s first party source. C - Data is comprehesive because it contains information about member type which is crucial for this analysis. However we may assume that there are many limitations because many variables which may have influence to customer prefference are not included in dataset. C - Data is current because it contains data from last 12 months. C - Data is also **cited* because it comes from first party source.

Process - Documentation of any cleaning or manipulation of data

Transforming data

  1. I will day and month columns separately so I can analyze data further.
Tripdata$month <-format(as.Date(Tripdata$started_at), "%m")
Tripdata$day <-format(as.Date(Tripdata$started_at), "%d")
Tripdata$dayoftheweek <-format(as.Date(Tripdata$started_at), "%A")
Tripdata$dayoftheweek <- factor(Tripdata$dayoftheweek, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  1. I will ad column with trip time
Tripdata$trip_time <- difftime(Tripdata$ended_at, Tripdata$started_at)

There’s a problem wit trip_time column - minimum value is under 0. With manager we decided to delete this data and analyze only rows with additive trip_time and also delete rows with null values mentioned at ROCC stage.

Tripdatav2 <- Tripdata %>% filter(trip_time > 0) %>% drop_na()

Cleaning reduced number of rows from 5 859 061 to 4 533 671

Analysis

During analysis I will use GGPLOT2 to see if there are any interesting data and correlations to show - keep in mind charts during this stage are draft charts and will be improved at next - share stage.

1.Number of trips per user type with rideable type categories - there are more members than casual riders, only casual riders use docked bikes

Tripdatav2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = rideable_type))

2.Pie charts of rideable type usage per user type - members use classic bikes instead of docked bikes, also casual riders use electric bikes little more often

Tripdatav2 %>%
  filter (member_casual == "casual") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, fill=rideable_type)) + geom_bar() + coord_polar(theta = "y")

Tripdatav2 %>%
  filter (member_casual == "member") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, fill=rideable_type)) + geom_bar() + coord_polar(theta = "y")

3.Avg trip time per user type (trip_time is in seconds so I divided it by 60 to see minutes) - casual riders spend more time riding a bike

Tripdatav2 %>%
ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y= trip_time/60)) + geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean")
## Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <difftime>.
## Defaulting to continuous.

4.Avg trip time per user type per rideable type - docked bikes are most time consuming for casual riders, as previously - casual riders spend more times riding a bike

Tripdatav2 %>%
ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y= trip_time/60, fill = member_casual)) + geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", position = "dodge")
## Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <difftime>.
## Defaulting to continuous.

5.Histogram of average trip time per user type (values limited to 1h and 2h because otherwise histogram couldn’t be visible) - most of rides are less than 20minutes but for casual riders we can see more longer rides

Tripdatav2 %>%
  filter(trip_time < 7200) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = trip_time/60)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~member_casual)
## Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <difftime>.
## Defaulting to continuous.
## `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.

Tripdatav2 %>%
  filter(trip_time < 3600) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = trip_time/60)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~member_casual)
## Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type <difftime>.
## Defaulting to continuous.
## `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.

Share - Supporting visualizations and key findings

Below there’s a HTML way to describe whole analysis but you can check also presentation here

Business task

Identify how do annual members and casual riders use Cyclistic bikes differently.

Members pay monthy subscriptions so they:

-don’t have to pay 1$ start fee

-don’t have to pay for classic bikes

-pay 0.17$ per min. for using electric bike instead of 0.42$ per min.

Dataset used

Data used for analysis is first-party data direcly from company’s tracking tool, it shows:

-type of bike used

-start and end date of the trip with separated days of the week and days of the month

-Trip time (created from start and end time of trip)

-User type: member and casual rider

-Cleaning the dataset from rows with NA values reduced number of rows from 5 859 061 to 4 533 671

Key finding from data

Members performed almost one million rides more over analyzed months

Tripdatav2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual)) + geom_bar(stat = "count", fill = "#02CDF1") + geom_label(stat = 'count', aes(label = ..count..)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) + labs(title = "Number of rides per user type", x ="", y= "") + theme_minimal()

Members use classic bikes instead of docked ones. Casual members have little more in electric bikes share

Act - top 3 recomendations based on analysis

Summarizing:

-Casual riders perform longer trips.

-Casual riders tend to use bikes more often on warm seasons, performing longer trips.

-Casual riders use more electric bikes in colder seasons.

-Casual riders use perform more rides on weekend when members perform more rides on working days.

What’s next?

-It’s good to see how weather affects bike usage

-Adding another subscription with cheaper electric bike renting prices would beneficent for casual riders

-Increasing renting prices for causal riders on weekend would put the subscription option in a favorable light

-Adding loyalty program which would give customers possibilities to earn free electric bike rides after certain amount of time would be motivating to buy a subscription
